en: Preface by the Disciple Monk Yong-sun to the Fourth Collection of the Record of Master Jue of Mount Langya in Chuzhou.

Regarding the masters who appear in the world and dwell in specific regions, they act with restraint; it is precisely for this reason that they uphold the guiding principles and shake the fundamental cords of the Dharma. Indeed, it is not... [text continues].
Having attained this, although he responded to the inclinations of the minds of the multitudes that came to him, was it not primarily here that he won over people?
Therefore, when our Chan Master of Langya appeared to transform the world, the four seas rushed toward him like clouds, reaching everywhere; his great voice resounded like a clap of thunder.
There was nothing he did not hear. Those who bore the weight of the sublime scriptures and profound treatises were surpassed by him in number;

they all hid their traces and silenced their voices in his presence. As for those who raised doctrines, each had its own ultimate aim, as he responded to movements and observed the capacities of beings.
No action is ever in vain. If someone is hindered by the literal words, I shall release them from their attachment;
if someone clings to their conceptual understanding, I shall remove their bondage. If someone remains stuck in the "upward" direction, I shall pull them back before it is too late;
if someone stagnates in the middle or lower stages, I shall strike them as soon as the signs appear. If there are deficiencies to be supplemented, I shall ensure that the True Eye is complete.

If one were to prune away its redundancies, the essential meaning would remain undisturbed. All [teachings] serve to detach from delusive emotions and extinguish the illumination of discursive wisdom;

only then does the true mind manifest before one, shining uniquely throughout antiquity and the present. According to the capacities of beings, they are established as expedients, yet all are gathered within a single flavor.
It is like the sun’s chariot at midday: its reflections appear boundlessly. When observers come from the four directions, it responds perfectly to each; how could it ever be fully exhausted?
The disciple Yuan Ju had long investigated the Master’s chamber and personally received his instructions; as these increased day by day, he recorded them.
In all, there were over a hundred items, which he subsequently compiled. To distinguish this from the previous and subsequent records, he titled it the "Middle Record.
Thus, by citing the preceding and succeeding [records], the middle is subsumed; by citing the middle, the preceding and succeeding are exhausted. It is not separate from them.
One proceeds from the former and the latter toward the middle; it is not that one leaves the middle to abide in the former and the latter. In the middle, there is neither after nor before;
in the former and the latter, there is no middle.
This is the great principle of the Master, which he penetrates with a single thread—how could it be grasped by mere thought? Even if one were to cast open one's eyes upon it...

Recently, it was as if one were wandering upon the vast blue sea, gazing at the palaces of the dragons; looking down upon the precious shells and gems, the mind and eyes were so brilliantly illuminated that there was no leisure to respond to them.

The details of my Master’s life circumstances, his studies, and his attainment of the Dharma are fully recorded in the separate biography (*bielu*), so I shall not trouble you with further accounts here.
As for the one who opened the treasury of the True Dharma Eye (*saddharmacakṣur-kośa*) and pointed directly to show others, he was none other than my Master.
